prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 1.4-6 Example of paving for comprehensive roads F. Smart city demonstration roads No special requirements

Spatial requirements: • It is recommended to reduce motor-vehicle traffic space as much as possible to provide space for non-motorized vehicles and pedestrians. Facility requirements: • Increase slow-mobility signage and pedestrian wayfinding signage to strengthen walkability. • Roadside municipal facilities such as traffic poles, lamp posts, and trash bins should be arranged in a rational manner to preserve the historic and cultural character of the streets and lanes. 12 Comprehensive roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Comprehensive roads are roads that combine multiple road-type characteristics, with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and may include roads with commercial and service functions as well as urban traffic functions. For comprehensive roads, the street design should be targeted according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. Spatial requirements: • Provide street-side spaces for dining and commercial services, as well as leisure and social interaction spaces. Where conditions permit, widen building setbacks to supplement pedestrian, green, and leisure areas. Facility requirements: • Provide continuous facilities, and arrange trees, leisure seating, outdoor display areas, self-parking spaces, roadside temporary parking, and roadside greenery in an integrated manner to facilitate residents’ daily activities. 13 Introduction 1. Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2. prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):
{
"scores": {
"justice": {
"overall": 68.0,
"equity": 70.0,
"fairness": 60.0,
"accessibility": 75.0
},
"safety": 72.0,
"livability": 65.0,
"sustainability": 58.0,
"aesthetics": 80.0,
"comfort": 62.0,
"walkability": 70.0
},
"explanations": {
"justice": [
"Wide sidewalks and ramps improve accessibility",
"Lack of tactile paving reduces fairness for visually impaired users",
"Sidewalk width is suitable for wheelchairs, reflecting equitable distribution"
],
"safety": [
"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",
"Limited visible lighting may reduce nighttime safety",
"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],
"livability": [
"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],
"sustainability": [
"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],
"aesthetics": [
"Uniform building heights and consistent facade designs create visual coherence",
"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}
 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. For comprehensive roads, the street design should be targeted according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. Spatial requirements: • Provide street-side spaces for dining and commercial services, as well as leisure and social interaction spaces. Where conditions permit, widen building setbacks to supplement pedestrian, green, and leisure areas. Facility requirements: • Provide continuous facilities, and arrange trees, leisure seating, outdoor display areas, self-parking spaces, roadside temporary parking, and roadside greenery in an integrated manner to facilitate residents’ daily activities. 13 Introduction 1. Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2.
